Relevance to WRRFs: Today, Python is the most common programming language in use for data science applied across multiple sectors (Github Staff 2024). In addition, it is open source and thrives on an active, global community of engineers, software developers, and scientists. Due to its popularity, commercial simulator software vendors active in the wastewater sector provide and support interfaces with their simulation packages. At the same time, Python supports interfacing with both legacy and modern data acquisition and control systems (e.g., SCADA systems, ROS) and database technologies, although security and variations in SCADA software provider standards require unique interfacing practices per utility (examples described below). Overall, we conclude that Python is the correct platform to develop WRRF specific tools for data mining, soft-sensing, and adaptive control, while maintaining access to the latest developments in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and model predictive control. SCADA systems are integral to WRRF operation and, therefore, the integration of Python and SCADA is an important consideration. As an outcome of this project, two architectures are proposed for integrating Python with SCADA systems and DCSs, modeled after Applications demonstrated at DC Water, HRSD, and Metro. At DC Water, the Python script was deployed directly to an edge device — a Raspberry Pi microcontroller. Once uploaded, the script received input data locally, executed the model, and sent the resulting outputs back to the control system. In contrast, HRSD and Metro implemented a centralized approach, running the Python scripts on a central server. At HRSD, inputs were transmitted to the server using Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC-UA), a common industrial communication standard. The model’s outputs were then returned to the control system over the same OPC-UA channel. Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 25 At Metro, the models were deployed on a remote Windows server located outside the SCADA firewall. The Python script used a basic request form (HTTP POST request) to both pull data from and push predictions to Metro’s data historian using the historian’s built-in application interface (API). By accessing data through the data historian, data from disparate sources can be retrieved using the same protocol despite being stored in different databases (i.e., read-only SCADA data and laboratory data). This method allowed Metro staff to view model outputs through existing dashboards and reporting tools without needing to modify or directly access the SCADA system. Because the server and laboratory database were positioned outside the SCADA network, this architecture maintained a strong cybersecurity boundary while still enabling integration of multiple data sources. These examples illustrate possible architectural options. Each utility must evaluate key factors when selecting an appropriate implementation strategy, such as whether the script requires only local inputs or signals from across the facility, how the model will be updated, and what cybersecurity measures are needed.
